text.p: Commodity prices slumped overnight, ending a month which saw most commodity prices, with the notable exception of oil, suffer steady erosion as a result of weak end-user demand and dwindling speculative interest as other markets like equities and bonds boomed.
The CRB index closed 1.01 points lower on the day at 245.63.
Gold was the latest to suffer, dropping to its lowest London fixing for a year at $379 an ounce. Gold began September at $387.
By contrast, benchmark North Sea crude oil futures are at their strongest since the 1991 Gulf War.

They rose above $23.50 per barrel during Monday on renewed Middle East tension and brisk demand for heating fuel to replenish low stocks. Extending a rally, they have put on some $3 over September as a whole.

Industrial metals had been expected to strengthen during the month, too, after the usual northern summer holiday lull in activity. But traders say that end-user demand has failed to live up to expectations.
Aluminium traded on Monday on the London Metal Exchange (LME) at its lowest for 2-1/4 years around $1,380 per tonne.
That compared with $1,515 at the beginning of September.

Grain prices earlier this year had more than matched the rally in crude oil. In March, after drought depressed world stocks to the lowest since the 1970s, the nearby Chicago Board of Trade wheat contract spiked to a record $7.50 per bushel.
Predictions of bigger crops this year later took the heat out of the rally and in September these were fulfilled as news of bumper European and Chinese harvests was reported.
CBOT wheat began September at almost $4.50 but ended month with December delivery at $4.36 and March at $422.50.

METALS - LME copper lost its nerve in the afternoon and ended near its lows after failing on the upside, pushing most other metals to fresh losses. Trading was frenzied on the kerb as lead dived to its lower level for nearly seven months and aluminium dropped to its lowest since June 1994. Three months copper finished the kerb at $1,928, down $29 from Friday and just $2.00 off its low for the day. Lead spiralled lwoer on the kerb, hitting $753, the lowest since March 7, and ended with a $22 loss at $756. Aluminium ended at $1,377.50, down $31.50 and only 50 cents off its low for the day. It was the weakest price since mid-June 1994 when the market hit $1,361. Nickel followed the trend, crashing below last week's range and hitting a low of $7,060. Prices however recovered to $7,100 by the end of the kerb, ending with a $110 loss. Zinc shed $8 to $1,016.

GOLD - New York precious metals futures ended sharply lower Monday, extending the decline of the past month, after gold bullion fixed in London Monday at its lowest level for more than a year at $379.00 an ounce. "U.S. dollar strength is depressing precious metal demand, particularly in Japan, while healthy U.S. equity and bond markets are providing no incentive for investors in precious metals either," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said. COMEX December gold ended down $2.30 an ounce at $380.50, after seeing a session low at $380.50, a new three year low for the December contract, while back months in gold saw life-of-contract lows. In New York bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted $378.20/378.60, after gold fixed at $379.00 in London Monday afternoon, the lowest fix since September 6, 1995.

GRAINS - CBOT wheat closed mixed with nearby contracts higher on bullish input from a USDA quarterly stocks report, traders said. Wheat futures closed 4-1/2 cents per bushel higher to 5-1/4 lower, with December up 4-1/2 at $4.36. March closed 1/2 higher at $4.22-1/2.

SUGAR - CSCE world sugar futures settled sharply firmer and near the day's highs on trade and speculative buying, dealers said. The most-active March contract closed up 0.22 at 10.89 a pound, having ranged from 10.94 to 10.72. Spot-October, which expires today, surged 0.43 on the day to close at 11.47.

OIL - The NYMEX oil complex ended mixed Monday as traders unraveled their positions in the expiring October refined products contract and took profits in crude after a top U.N. aide expressed hope for the Iraq "oil-for-food" deal. November crude hit a contract high of $24.80 a barrel, but it settled 22 cents lower at $24.38 after United Nations Under Secretary General Yasushi Akashi said he hoped the Iraq oil-for-food deal could go ahead in the near future. Akashi told a news conference in Geneva Monday that the world body was assessing whether all conditions had been met for the suspended deal to be implemented.
